lesson.title: What Are We Actually Measuring? Introducing Variables
lesson.summary: This section defines a variable as a characteristic that can take different values across the individuals in a dataset, and shows how the classroom data from the previous section is organized into variables.
lesson.body:
Once you have data, the next question is: data about what, exactly? A variable is any characteristic, number, or quantity that can be measured or recorded, and that takes different values across the individuals being studied. The word "variable" comes from the same root as "vary," and that is the whole idea: a variable is something that varies from one observation to the next. If every student in a class had exactly the same height, height would not be a useful variable to record, because it would carry no information that distinguishes one student from another.

Go back to the classroom data introduced in the previous section. The teacher did not just record a pile of unconnected numbers. She recorded two specific characteristics for each of the 8 students: quiz score and height. Quiz score is a variable because it varies from student to student, ranging from 5 to 10 points in this class. Height is a separate variable, also varying from student to student. Each variable has a name, and each variable has a set of possible values it could take. Quiz score, in this case, could reasonably take any whole number value from 0 to 10. Height could take any positive number of inches within a realistic human range.

It helps to keep two things separate in your mind: the variable itself and a specific value of that variable. "Quiz score" is the variable, the general characteristic being measured. "7" is a value of that variable, the specific number recorded for one particular student. This distinction becomes important once you start doing calculations, because formulas in statistics are written in terms of variables in general, and you plug in specific values from your dataset to get a specific numeric answer.

As a worked example, look again at the 8 recorded quiz scores: 7, 8, 6, 9, 7, 5, 8, 10. The variable here is quiz score, and it takes 8 specific values across the 8 students in the dataset, one value per student. The range of this variable, meaning the difference between its largest and smallest recorded value, is 10 minus 5, which equals 5 points. Reporting the range is one of the simplest things you can do with a variable: it tells you how spread out the recorded values are, without yet requiring anything as sophisticated as an average.

Not all variables behave the same way, and later sections will draw an important line between two broad types. Categorical variables sort individuals into named groups, like the eye color or favorite subject of each student. Quantitative variables assign each individual a number that can be used in arithmetic, like quiz score or height. Recognizing which type of variable you are dealing with is one of the very first decisions you make in any statistical analysis, because it determines which summaries, graphs, and calculations are even appropriate to use.
